10: +### Purpose
11:  
12:  Code work is not one activity. Writing code needs author-side quality gates and comment hygiene. Reviewing it needs a findings-first baseline with security and correctness checks. CI workflow work needs trigger, permission and job-shape rules. System work needs hook and alignment verification. Each kind of code work carries its own contract, yet they all share the same surface identity rules.
13:  
14:  Without one routing point, every contract would duplicate surface detection and a request that touches several kinds of code work would have no ordered way to resolve. sk-code exists so one advisor identity covers the whole code family: the hub centralizes surface detection once and routes each request to the focused packet that owns the work.

Use a mode hint when you already know the contract you need and let the hub classify when the request spans intents.
19: +

22:  `Skill(sk-code)` loads the hub. The hub routes the request through `mode-registry.json` to one of two workflow modes. Root `ROUTER.md` then selects the packet leaves and declared shared controls bundled alongside it. Each mode and surface holds its own code-work contract while the hub itself stays routing-only. 17: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
18: 
19: | Aspect | What you get |
20: |---|---|
21: | **Use it for** | Code-family work: implementation, quality gating, debugging, verification and findings-first review |
22: | **Invoke with** | `Skill(sk-code)` plus an optional mode hint such as `sk-code-quality:` or `sk-code-review:` |
23: | **Works on** | The shared surface-detection router for the three surfaces the hub `SKILL.md` lists: the native SKILLED surface, the `sk-code-ci` CI standards surface and the stack-agnostic `sk-code-frontend` surface |
24: | **Produces** | A routed workflow mode or bundled surface evidence packet with the matching code-work contract and tool surface. The quality and review modes work in any repository and read that repository's own rule overrides |
25: 
26: ---
27: 
28: ## 2. OVERVIEW
29: 
30: ### Purpose
31: 
32: Code work is not one activity. Writing code needs author-side quality gates and comment hygiene. Reviewing it needs a findings-first baseline with security and correctness checks. CI workflow work needs trigger, permission and job-shape rules. System work needs hook and alignment verification. Each kind of code work carries its own contract, yet they all share the same surface identity rules.
33: 
34: Without one routing point, every contract would duplicate surface detection and a request that touches several kinds of code work would have no ordered way to resolve. sk-code exists so one advisor identity covers the whole code family: the hub centralizes surface detection once and routes each request to the focused packet that owns the work.
35: 
36: ### When to Use
37: 
38: Reach for sk-code when the task is code work and the next step is implementation, author-side quality, debugging, verification or review. Shared stack detection tries every declared specific surface first, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN. A skill outside the hub that names family sk-code can declare its own `surface_detection` block in `graph-metadata.json` and outrank SKILLED. The CI surface is bundled from request vocabulary, not from detection (see `shared/references/stack-detection.md`). Use a mode hint when you already know the contract you need and let the hub classify when the request spans intents.
39: 
40: ### What It Does
41: 
42: `Skill(sk-code)` loads the hub. The hub routes the request through `mode-registry.json` to one of two workflow modes. Root `ROUTER.md` then selects the packet leaves and declared shared controls bundled alongside it. Each mode and surface holds its own code-work contract while the hub itself stays routing-only. The packets carry no `graph-metadata.json`, so the advisor discovers exactly one code skill.
43: 
44: The boundary is deliberate: sk-code routes code work. Documentation quality, git workflow, spec discipline and browser evidence belong to sibling skills that sk-code hands off to.
45: 
46: ### The Code Work Contract Grid
47: 
48: **Workflow modes (act):**
49: 
50: | Mode | Owns | Pointer |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | `sk-code-quality` | Author-side quality gates, comment hygiene and surface checklists, with a hard floor and rules a repository can change | [`README.md`](./sk-code-quality/README.md) |
53: | `sk-code-review` | Findings-first review: a fixed security and correctness floor, a default lens a repository can change, review output cache | [`README.md`](./sk-code-review/README.md) |
54: 
55: **Surface evidence packets (read-only and advisor-invisible, bundled alongside a workflow mode):**
56: 
57: | Surface | Carries | Pointer |
58: |---|---|---|
59: | `sk-code-ci` | GitHub Actions workflow standards: trigger and filter rules, job shape, the protected set and the scaffold templates | [`README.md`](./sk-code-ci/README.md) |
60: | `sk-code-frontend` | Stack-agnostic web practice, topic references, and Figma-to-code checks | [`README.md`](./sk-code-frontend/README.md) |
61: | `sk-code-skilled` | Native surface. System-code evidence: TypeScript, Python, shell and config standards, hooks, alignment verification, authoring checklists | [`README.md`](./sk-code-skilled/README.md) |
62: 
63: ---
64: 
65: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
66: 
67: ### How A Request Resolves
68: 
69: A code request resolves through the hub to a primary workflow mode and one or more bundled surface packets. A request that spans intents stays at the hub for ordered routing or disambiguation. These examples show the shape of a resolution:
70: 
71: | Request | Resolves to |
72: |---|---|
73: | "review my typescript module for jank" | `[sk-code-review, sk-code-skilled]` |
74: | "review the github actions workflow yaml" | `[sk-code-review, sk-code-ci]` |
75: | "run my implementation through the author-side quality gates" | `[sk-code-quality]` |
76: 
77: ### The Implement To Verify Doctrine
78: 
79: The implement → debug → verify phases are not standalone modes. Their surface-agnostic doctrine lives once in `shared/references/`, symlinked into each surface so the active surface carries the full workflow without duplicating it:
80: 
81: - `workflow-implement.md` for the authoring pass
82: - `workflow-debug.md` for the repair pass
83: - `workflow-verify.md` for the proof pass
84: 
85: ### Rules A Repository Can Change
86: 
87: The quality and review modes ship defaults, and a repository does not have to accept them. Each rule has an id. A small hard floor is fixed everywhere: secrets, conflict markers, parse failures, input validation, silent failures, initialization safety, resource cleanup, accessibility for UI code, and the review severity ids, reach rule and security and correctness minimums. Every other rule can be dropped or replaced.
88: 
89: A repository does that in a `## Rule overrides` section of a checklist its quality config names, and a surface does it in the checklists its declaration names.
90: 
91: - Both modes read the same section through one linter, so a rule dropped for quality does not return as a review finding.
92: - A quality run applies the section of every checklist it loads: a refused section or an unknown rule id is `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3, each accepted row is recorded in the run's decisions, and two checklists at one level that disagree make the rule unverified.
93: - `commentHygiene.disableRules` in the quality config switches off named comment-hygiene rules for the runner, the pre-commit hook and the CI job together.
94: 
95: The contract is [`shared/references/universal/rule-overrides.md`](./shared/references/universal/rule-overrides.md), and this framework's own house style lives in the SKILLED surface so a foreign repository does not inherit it.
96: 
97: ### One Advisor Identity
98: 
99: The mode packets and `shared/` carry no `graph-metadata.json` of their own. The hub root keeps the single graph identity for the whole family. `mode-registry.json` is the routing source of truth while `hub-router.json` preserves the vocabulary that helps code prompts resolve to the right mode.
100:

102: 
103: ## 4. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
104: 
105: ### Related Skills
106: 
107: | Skill | Relationship |
108: |---|---|
109: | `sk-design-md-generator` | Extracts a measured Style Reference (design tokens from a live source) that sk-code may implement |
110: | `sk-design-fundamentals` | When a request or a frame leaves a visual value open (spacing, type, color, radius, shadow or motion), or a value sits off every token and scale, load `sk-design-fundamentals` and decide it there. |
111: | `sk-doc` | Owns markdown and documentation quality |
112: | `sk-git` | Owns branches, commits, PRs and the finish workflow |
113: | `system-spec-kit` | Owns spec folders, memory, continuity and packet validation |
114: | `mcp-chrome-devtools` | Provides browser evidence for frontend runtime behavior |
115: 
116: ---
117: 
118: ## 5. ADAPTING TO YOUR STACK
119: 
120: sk-code ships three surfaces:
121: 
122: - **CI** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/`): the GitHub Actions workflow rules and their evidence. Its references say which values (switch names, protected workflows, branches) come from the repository's own CI profile at `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/repository/ci.json`.
123: - **Frontend** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/`): stack-agnostic web practice, topic references and Figma-to-code checks.
124: - **Skilled** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/`): the native standards for this framework's own code, so keep it.
125: 
126: A surface you add for your own stack ranks ahead of the Skilled surface. Run every command below from the repository root.
127: 
128: ### Before You Start
129: 
130: 1. In a fresh clone, run `bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh provision .` first. It installs the dependencies and builds the spec-kit outputs the checks below load. Without it, `parent-skill-check.cjs` and `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs` fail on a missing `@spec-kit/shared` build.
131: 2. In a clone, run `git config --local skilled.trustRepoHooks true` before you install the hooks. The hooks run this repository's scripts only in a trusted clone, so without it the commit-time re-mint never fires.
132: 3. Install the git hooks with `bash .skilled/scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`. A commit that stages the hub's routing files then re-mints its activation manifest and copies the manifest to its authored path. Without the hooks, do both by hand after each routing change: run `node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-manifest.cjs refresh --hub sk-code --skill-root .skilled/skills/sk-code`, then copy `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json` over `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json`.
133: 4. If you prune `specs/`, keep `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/`, the authored source of compiled routing, and keep the `.opencode/skills` link. Without either one the guard and sync checks fail.
134: 
135: ### Remove A Surface
136: 
137: Repeat these steps for each surface you drop. `<mode>` is the folder name of the surface packet.
138: 
139: 1. Delete the folder `.skilled/skills/sk-code/<mode>/`.
140: 2. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json`, delete the mode's `modes` entry and its name in `extensions.surface-axis.surfaces`. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/hub-router.json`, delete it from `routerPolicy.tieBreak`, delete its `routerSignals` entry and delete the two `vocabularyClasses` that entry names.
141: 3. Regenerate the leaf manifest with `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write .skilled/skills/sk-code`.
142: 4. Edit section 8 of `.skilled/skills/sk-code/ROUTER.md` by hand, because no command writes it. Delete every `RESOURCE_MAP` path under `<mode>/`, then delete each key left with no paths from both `RESOURCE_MAP` and `INTENT_SIGNALS`. Trim the prose map rows and sections above section 8 that point at the removed packet.
143: 5. Update the surface table and the surface list sentence in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/SKILL.md`, the mode's `surfaceDetection` block in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json` (`stack-detection.md` section 2 reads it) and the surface lines in the root `README.md`.
144: 6. Delete or adjust the files written for the surface. These are its scenarios under `.skilled/skills/sk-code/manual-testing-playbook/`, with their rows in `manual-testing-playbook.md`, the surface checklist pointers in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/`, the entries in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/feature-catalog.md` and `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/two-axis-registry-driven-routing/two-axis-registry-driven-routing.md`, which name each live surface, the cases in `.skilled/bin/tests/compiled-route-surface-hint.test.cjs` and the canary cases that name the mode in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`. After a canary edit, copy that fixture over its authored twin at `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`.
145: 7. Run `node .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/verify-doc-claims.cjs` and fix every dead path and stale surface count it lists, including those in this README. Then run `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/regenerate-skill-derived.cjs --root .skilled/skills/sk-code --write`, which prunes the dead `key_files`, `source_docs` and entities from the hub's `graph-metadata.json`. The only hand edit left in that file is its `causal_summary`, which names each surface.
146: 8. Refresh the README manifest with `python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/tests/test_readme_manifest.py --write`, and the Hermes skill copies with `node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/hermes/sync-skills-hermes.cjs`, which drops the removed packet's copy.
147: 9. Commit with the hooks installed, or refresh and copy the manifest by hand as above.
148: 
149: ### Add Your Own Surface
150: 
151: 1. Run `/create:skill-parent update --surfaces <name>` in your AI runtime. Its steps live in `.skilled/commands/create/assets/create-skill-parent-auto.yaml`. It scaffolds the packet, registers it and places it ahead of `sk-code-skilled` in `tieBreak`, so your surface wins a keyword tie. If you edit `tieBreak` by hand instead, keep your surface ahead of `sk-code-skilled`, because the doctor's check 5l warns about a surface placed after it, and the registry compiler rejects a hub whose single fallback is not ranked last in `routerPolicy.tieBreak` (`SURFACE_FALLBACK_INVALID`).
152: 2. Link the three shared workflow docs into the new packet the way `sk-code-skilled/references/` does: in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/<name>/references/`, symlink `workflow-implement.md`, `workflow-debug.md` and `workflow-verify.md` to the files of the same name in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/references/` (link target `../../shared/references/<file>`).
153: 3. Add the packet's paths to the `ROUTER.md` maps and section 8, and its `surfaceDetection` block to its `mode-registry.json` entry (`stack-detection.md` section 2 reads it). Update any surface-count wording that `verify-doc-claims.cjs` checks in the hub's `README.md` and `SKILL.md`. `phase-detection.md` names the surfaces without a count. A packet copied from an existing surface has the same leaf set as that surface, so `generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write` stops with `MODE_LEAF_SET_COLLISION`. Give each of the two modes its own `leafScopes` in a new `leaf-scopes.json` at the hub root, in the array format `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/leaf-scopes.json` uses, or change the copy until its files differ.
154: 4. Add a canary case that routes to the new surface in the canary fixture above, and copy the fixture over its authored twin. The completion report of the update command names both follow-ups.
155: 5. Refresh the Hermes skill copies the same way, then commit with the hooks installed, or refresh and copy the manifest by hand.
156: 
157: ### Add a Private Surface Outside the Hub
158: 
159: A surface you keep out of the repository lives in its own skill beside the hub instead of inside it.
160: 
161: 1. Create the skill folder as `.skilled/skills/local-<name>/`. Git ignores every `local-*` skill, so the folder and its standards stay in your checkout. It can be a symlink to a folder in another repository.
162: 2. In the skill's own `graph-metadata.json`, set `"family": "sk-code"` and add a top-level `surface_detection` block with a `label`, `"role": "specific"` and at least one of `pathMarkers`, `fileMarkers` and `contentMarkers`. The example and the rules are in `shared/references/stack-detection.md`, under "Declaring an External Surface".
163: 3. Check the block by hand against those rules. `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs` skips folders whose name starts with `local-`, so no check validates it for you.
164: 4. If the folder is a symlink whose target sits outside `.skilled/skills/`, add a folder that contains that target to `SPECKIT_PRIVATE_SKILL_ROOTS` for every advisor process. Without it, the advisor skips the skill.
165: 
166: Stack detection tries the hub's own specific surfaces first, then the surfaces that skills outside the hub declare, sorted by skill id, and SKILLED last as the fallback. Nothing in the hub's registry, router or tracked files names the private skill.
167: 
168: ### Verify The Result
169: 
170: Each of these must exit 0. Then route a prompt that names your stack, and check that your surface comes first.
171: 
172: ```bash
173: node .skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/parent-skill-check.cjs .skilled/skills/sk-code
174: node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs
175: node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-guard.cjs
176: node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-sync.cjs --check
177: bash .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/scripts/run-all-drift-guards.sh
178: node .skilled/bin/compiled-route.cjs --hub sk-code --prompt "<a prompt about your stack>"
179: ```
180: 
181: - `/doctor:sk-code setup` runs these legs in one read-only pass, adds the derived-metadata freshness check CI runs, a provisioning precheck and a quality leg that checks the quality runner is ready, fails the route probe when it returns the legacy stub and prints one repair command for each failing leg.
182: - `/doctor:sk-code quality` shows which quality config the gate reads, checks it, names the comment-hygiene rules it switches off, and when there is none it creates the quality config the `sk-code-quality` packet holds, once after you approve.
183: - Outside an AI runtime, run `node .skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/sk-code-setup-check.cjs`.
184: - For GitHub Actions workflows, `/doctor:ci report` lists each workflow's switch state and drift flags, and `/doctor:ci scaffold` or `/doctor:ci toggle` apply the CI surface's templates and switches after you say yes.
185: 
186: ---
187: 
188: ## 6. FAQ
189: 
190: **Q: Why does the advisor see only one code skill when the hub contains a packet per mode and surface?**
191: 
192: A: The mode packets and `shared/` carry no `graph-metadata.json` of their own. The hub root holds the single graph identity for the whole family, so prompts resolve to one entry point and the hub routes from there.
193: 
194: **Q: What happens when a request spans intents, like review plus implementation?**
195: 
196: A: The request stays at the hub. The hub orders the routing and asks for disambiguation instead of guessing a single mode.
197:

203: |---|---|

91: - Both modes read the same section through one linter, so a rule dropped for quality does not return as a review finding.
92: - A quality run applies the section of every checklist it loads: a refused section or an unknown rule id is `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3, each accepted row is recorded in the run's decisions, and two checklists at one level that disagree make the rule unverified.
93: - `commentHygiene.disableRules` in the quality config switches off named comment-hygiene rules for the runner, the pre-commit hook and the CI job together.
94: 
95: The contract is [`shared/references/universal/rule-overrides.md`](./shared/references/universal/rule-overrides.md), and this framework's own house style lives in the SKILLED surface so a foreign repository does not inherit it.
96: 
97: ### One Advisor Identity
98: 
99: The mode packets and `shared/` carry no `graph-metadata.json` of their own. The hub root keeps the single graph identity for the whole family. `mode-registry.json` is the routing source of truth while `hub-router.json` preserves the vocabulary that helps code prompts resolve to the right mode.

117: 
118: ## 5. ADAPTING TO YOUR STACK
119: 
120: sk-code ships three surfaces:
121: 
122: - **CI** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/`): the GitHub Actions workflow rules and their evidence. Its references say which values (switch names, protected workflows, branches) come from the repository's own CI profile at `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-ci/repository/ci.json`.
123: - **Frontend** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/`): stack-agnostic web practice, topic references and Figma-to-code checks.
124: - **Skilled** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/`): the native standards for this framework's own code, so keep it.
125: 
126: A surface you add for your own stack ranks ahead of the Skilled surface. Run every command below from the repository root.
127: 
128: ### Before You Start
129: 
130: 1. In a fresh clone, run `bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh provision .` first. It installs the dependencies and builds the spec-kit outputs the checks below load. 131: 2. In a clone, run `git config --local skilled.trustRepoHooks true` before you install the hooks. The hooks run this repository's scripts only in a trusted clone, so without it the commit-time re-mint never fires.
132: 3. Install the git hooks with `bash .skilled/scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`. A commit that stages the hub's routing files then re-mints its activation manifest and copies the manifest to its authored path. Without the hooks, do both by hand after each routing change: run `node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-manifest.cjs refresh --hub sk-code --skill-root .skilled/skills/sk-code`, then copy `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json` over `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json`.
133: 4. If you prune `specs/`, keep `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/`, the authored source of compiled routing, and keep the `.opencode/skills` link. Without either one the guard and sync checks fail.

136:

138:

140: 2. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json`, delete the mode's `modes` entry and its name in `extensions.surface-axis.surfaces`. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/hub-router.json`, delete it from `routerPolicy.tieBreak`, delete its `routerSignals` entry and delete the two `vocabularyClasses` that entry names.

Trim the prose map rows and sections above section 8 that point at the removed packet.

144: 6. Delete or adjust the files written for the surface. These are its scenarios under `.skilled/skills/sk-code/manual-testing-playbook/`, with their rows in `manual-testing-playbook.md`, the surface checklist pointers in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/`, the entries in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/feature-catalog.md` and `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/two-axis-registry-driven-routing/two-axis-registry-driven-routing.md`, which name each live surface, the cases in `.skilled/bin/tests/compiled-route-surface-hint.test.cjs` and the canary cases that name the mode in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`. Update any surface-count wording that `verify-doc-claims.cjs` checks in the hub's `README.md` and `SKILL.md`. `phase-detection.md` names the surfaces without a count. A packet copied from an existing surface has the same leaf set as that surface, so `generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write` stops with `MODE_LEAF_SET_COLLISION`. 159: A surface you keep out of the repository lives in its own skill beside the hub instead of inside it.

161: 1. Create the skill folder as `.skilled/skills/local-<name>/`. Git ignores every `local-*` skill, so the folder and its standards stay in your checkout. It can be a symlink to a folder in another repository.

14: # Phase Detection and Lifecycle
15: 
16: Every sk-code task that changes code moves through the same gated phases, from research to verified completion. Open it when the next move is unclear: which phase a task is in, which doctrine owns it, or what evidence ends it.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Keep research, implementation, the quality gate, debugging and verification in a fixed order, so no task reaches "done" on a skipped gate. The active surface changes which resources and evidence each phase uses. It never changes the order or the gates.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Planning code work on any sk-code surface.
29: - Choosing which phase doctrine and checklists to load next.
30: - Routing a failed quality or verification gate back to debugging or implementation.
31: - Judging whether the completion evidence is enough to claim "done".
32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: A phase ends on evidence, not on effort. The next phase starts only when the current one has produced what its exit condition names.
36: 
37: ### Key Sources
38: 
39: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) selects the surface. It returns SKILLED or UNKNOWN and never `sk-code-ci` or `sk-code-frontend`, which the hub bundles from request vocabulary alone (`code-ci-aliases` and `code-ci-runtime`, and `code-frontend-aliases`, in `hub-router.json`).
40: - `mode-registry.json` declares the workflow modes (`sk-code-quality`, `sk-code-review`) and the surfaces (`sk-code-ci`, `sk-code-frontend`, `sk-code-skilled`).
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. PHASE MAP
45: 
46: ```text
47: Phase 0   Research        optional for simple edits, required for complex or risky work
48: Phase 1   Implementation
49: Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate
50: Phase 2   Debugging       entered when a check fails
51: Phase 3   Verification
52: done      only with recorded verification evidence
53: ```
54: 
55: Implement, debug and verify are not modes. Their doctrine lives once in `shared/references/workflow-*.md`, and each surface reaches it through a symlink in its own `references/` folder.
56: 
57: | Phase | Owner | What the phase produces |
58: | --- | --- | --- |
59: | 0 Research | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) §2 Research | Target files read, every place the change must reach listed, a plan |
60: | 1 Implementation | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) | The smallest correct change, plus a baseline and blast-radius note |
61: | 1.5 Code Quality Gate | `sk-code-quality` mode, [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) | P0 items pass, P1 items fixed or approved for deferral |
62: | 2 Debugging | [workflow-debug.md](./workflow-debug.md) | A named root cause and a fix that addresses that one cause |
63: | 3 Verification | [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md) | Fresh command output, exit codes and the delta from baseline |
64: 
65: `sk-code-review` runs outside this lifecycle. It writes no tracked file, so it has no Phase 1 and reports findings instead.
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. PER-SURFACE EVIDENCE
70: 
71: Surface precedence decides which table applies. `sk-code-skilled` is the fallback surface and is checked last. Any other surface that matches the task outranks it, including a private `local-*` surface skill where one is installed. When no surface matches, the surface is UNKNOWN and iron law 3 applies.
72: 
73: ### SKILLED (`sk-code-skilled`)
74: 
75: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
76: | --- | --- |
77: | 0 Research | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/`, the affected skill, agent or command and the bound spec folder |
78: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/` plus the detected language folders from [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) §3 |
79: | 1.5 Code Quality | `sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/universal-checklist.md` plus the checklist for each touched language |
80: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output, language-specific patterns |
81: | 3 Verification | The drift-guard umbrella, plus targeted tests and spec validation |
82: 
83: The drift-guard umbrella runs four guards in one pass: alignment drift, stack folders, router sync and doc claims. It prints one PASS or FAIL line per guard and exits non-zero if any fails.
84: 
85: ```bash
86: bash .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/scripts/run-all-drift-guards.sh
87: ```
88: 
89: ### CI (`sk-code-ci`)
90: 
91: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
92: | --- | --- |
93: | 0 Research | `sk-code-ci/references/protected-set.md`, then the workflow files the change touches |
94: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-ci/assets/workflow-template.yml` or `job-block-template.yml`, plus the trigger, filter and job-shape rules |
95: | 1.5 Code Quality | The rule index in `sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` |
96: | 2 Debugging | The failing workflow run and the rule it broke |
97: | 3 Verification | The machine gate the rule index names for each rule, plus a reviewer read for every honour-system rule |
98: 
99: The CI surface writes nothing. The acting agent applies its rules, and a rule the index marks honour-system has no check behind it, so only a careful read catches a lapse.
100: 
101: ### Frontend (`sk-code-frontend`)
102: 
103: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
104: | --- | --- |
105: | 0 Research | `sk-code-frontend/references/frontend-practice.md`, then the markup, style or component files the change touches and the design it must match |
106: | 1 Implementation | The same core, then `sk-code-frontend/references/web-markup-and-css.md`, then the one `web-*.md` topic file whose condition in the surface router applies |
107: | 1.5 Code Quality | The surface carries no checklist, so the gate stays with `sk-code-quality` and its universal floor |
108: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output and the stack layer or topic file that owns the behavior |
109: | 3 Verification | `sk-code-frontend/references/figma-to-code.md` where a built screen is compared with its Figma frame, plus the repository's own commands for that stack |
110: 
111: The Frontend surface writes nothing either. The acting mode applies its guidance, and a Figma pass that cannot run is marked `NOT RUN` with its reason, so the overall verdict is `INCOMPLETE`.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. IRON LAWS
116: 
117: These hold on every surface and in every mode. No phase transition relaxes them.
118: 
119: 1. **No completion claim without Phase 3 verification evidence.** A clean read, a green unit test or a successful build each prove less than the claim "it works", so only fresh verification output counts.
120: 2. **No Phase 1 completion claim without the Phase 1.5 quality gate.** Written code is unreviewed code until its P0 items pass.
121: 3. **No claim about an unsupported surface.** An UNKNOWN surface gets:
122:    - the universal floor in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md),
123:    - the quality runner's built-in checks,
124:    - the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names,
125:    - each with its overrides applied under [rule-overrides.md](./universal/rule-overrides.md).
126: 
127:    That config can come from `--config`, the git config key `skcode.qualityConfig` or `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet, and it never supplies a verification command, so the command set still comes from [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md), which asks for it. The spec-folder authoring checklist applies only where the SKILLED surface resolves. No other standard and no discovered command applies.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ## 5. TRANSITIONS
132: 
133: | From | To | Condition |
134: | --- | --- | --- |
135: | 0 | 1 | Enough context and a plan exist. For implementation intent, the Phase 0 to 1 gate also requires choosing the laziest viable rung of the Design Restraint Ladder in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) before any new code |
136: | 1 | 1.5 | Code was written or changed |
137: | 1.5 | 2 | A P0 quality issue or a failing check was found |
138: | 2 | 1.5 | A fix was applied, so the gate runs again on the changed code |
139: | 1.5 | 3 | Every P0 item passes, and each P1 item is fixed or approved for deferral |
140: | 3 | 1 | Verification finds required behavior missing or build work incomplete |
141: | 3 | 1.5 | An author-side check, comment hygiene or a checklist issue blocks verification |
142: | 3 | 2 | A command, runtime check or test fails, or a test proves nothing |
143: | 3 | done | Verification evidence is recorded |
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ## 6. RELATED RESOURCES
148: 
149: - [ROUTER.md](../../ROUTER.md) maps intent to resources and declares this file part of the always-loaded preamble.
150: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) covers surface detection and SKILLED language sub-detection.
151: - [`../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md) runs the Phase 1.5 gate.
152: - [`../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md) holds the CI rule evidence and the protected set.
153: - [`../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md) holds the frontend core, the web stack layer and the Figma-to-code check.

32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: A phase ends on evidence, not on effort. The next phase starts only when the current one has produced what its exit condition names.
36: 
37: ### Key Sources
38: 
39: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) selects the surface. It returns SKILLED or UNKNOWN and never `sk-code-ci` or `sk-code-frontend`, which the hub bundles from request vocabulary alone (`code-ci-aliases` and `code-ci-runtime`, and `code-frontend-aliases`, in `hub-router.json`).
40: - `mode-registry.json` declares the workflow modes (`sk-code-quality`, `sk-code-review`) and the surfaces (`sk-code-ci`, `sk-code-frontend`, `sk-code-skilled`).
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. PHASE MAP
45: 
46: ```text
47: Phase 0   Research        optional for simple edits, required for complex or risky work
48: Phase 1   Implementation
49: Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate
50: Phase 2   Debugging       entered when a check fails
51: Phase 3   Verification
52: done      only with recorded verification evidence
53: ```
54: 
55: Implement, debug and verify are not modes. Their doctrine lives once in `shared/references/workflow-*.md`, and each surface reaches it through a symlink in its own `references/` folder.
56: 
57: | Phase | Owner | What the phase produces |
58: | --- | --- | --- |
59: | 0 Research | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) §2 Research | Target files read, every place the change must reach listed, a plan |
60: | 1 Implementation | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) | The smallest correct change, plus a baseline and blast-radius note |
61: | 1.5 Code Quality Gate | `sk-code-quality` mode, [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) | P0 items pass, P1 items fixed or approved for deferral |
62: | 2 Debugging | [workflow-debug.md](./workflow-debug.md) | A named root cause and a fix that addresses that one cause |
63: | 3 Verification | [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md) | Fresh command output, exit codes and the delta from baseline |
64: 
65: `sk-code-review` runs outside this lifecycle. It writes no tracked file, so it has no Phase 1 and reports findings instead.
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. PER-SURFACE EVIDENCE
70: 
71: Surface precedence decides which table applies. `sk-code-skilled` is the fallback surface and is checked last. Any other surface that matches the task outranks it, including a private `local-*` surface skill where one is installed. When no surface matches, the surface is UNKNOWN and iron law 3 applies.
72: 
73: ### SKILLED (`sk-code-skilled`)
74: 
75: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
76: | --- | --- |
77: | 0 Research | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/`, the affected skill, agent or command and the bound spec folder |
78: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/` plus the detected language folders from [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) §3 |
79: | 1.5 Code Quality | `sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/universal-checklist.md` plus the checklist for each touched language |
80: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output, language-specific patterns |
81: | 3 Verification | The drift-guard umbrella, plus targeted tests and spec validation |
82: 
83: The drift-guard umbrella runs four guards in one pass: alignment drift, stack folders, router sync and doc claims. It prints one PASS or FAIL line per guard and exits non-zero if any fails.
84: 
85: ```bash
86: bash .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/scripts/run-all-drift-guards.sh
87: ```
88: 
89: ### CI (`sk-code-ci`)
90: 
91: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
92: | --- | --- |
93: | 0 Research | `sk-code-ci/references/protected-set.md`, then the workflow files the change touches |
94: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-ci/assets/workflow-template.yml` or `job-block-template.yml`, plus the trigger, filter and job-shape rules |
95: | 1.5 Code Quality | The rule index in `sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` |
96: | 2 Debugging | The failing workflow run and the rule it broke |
97: | 3 Verification | The machine gate the rule index names for each rule, plus a reviewer read for every honour-system rule |
98: 
99: The CI surface writes nothing. The acting agent applies its rules, and a rule the index marks honour-system has no check behind it, so only a careful read catches a lapse.
100: 
101: ### Frontend (`sk-code-frontend`)
102: 
103: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
104: | --- | --- |
105: | 0 Research | `sk-code-frontend/references/frontend-practice.md`, then the markup, style or component files the change touches and the design it must match |
106: | 1 Implementation | The same core, then `sk-code-frontend/references/web-markup-and-css.md`, then the one `web-*.md` topic file whose condition in the surface router applies |
107: | 1.5 Code Quality | The surface carries no checklist, so the gate stays with `sk-code-quality` and its universal floor |
108: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output and the stack layer or topic file that owns the behavior |
109: | 3 Verification | `sk-code-frontend/references/figma-to-code.md` where a built screen is compared with its Figma frame, plus the repository's own commands for that stack |
110: 
111: The Frontend surface writes nothing either. The acting mode applies its guidance, and a Figma pass that cannot run is marked `NOT RUN` with its reason, so the overall verdict is `INCOMPLETE`.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. IRON LAWS
116: 
117: These hold on every surface and in every mode. No phase transition relaxes them.
118: 
119: 1. **No completion claim without Phase 3 verification evidence.** A clean read, a green unit test or a successful build each prove less than the claim "it works", so only fresh verification output counts.
120: 2. **No Phase 1 completion claim without the Phase 1.5 quality gate.** Written code is unreviewed code until its P0 items pass.
121: 3. **No claim about an unsupported surface.** An UNKNOWN surface gets:
122:    - the universal floor in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md),
123:    - the quality runner's built-in checks,
124:    - the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names,
125:    - each with its overrides applied under [rule-overrides.md](./universal/rule-overrides.md).
126: 
127:    That config can come from `--config`, the git config key `skcode.qualityConfig` or `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet, and it never supplies a verification command, so the command set still comes from [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md), which asks for it. The spec-folder authoring checklist applies only where the SKILLED surface resolves. No other standard and no discovered command applies.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ## 5. TRANSITIONS
132: 
133: | From | To | Condition |
134: | --- | --- | --- |
135: | 0 | 1 | Enough context and a plan exist. For implementation intent, the Phase 0 to 1 gate also requires choosing the laziest viable rung of the Design Restraint Ladder in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) before any new code |
136: | 1 | 1.5 | Code was written or changed |
137: | 1.5 | 2 | A P0 quality issue or a failing check was found |
138: | 2 | 1.5 | A fix was applied, so the gate runs again on the changed code |
139: | 1.5 | 3 | Every P0 item passes, and each P1 item is fixed or approved for deferral |
140: | 3 | 1 | Verification finds required behavior missing or build work incomplete |
141: | 3 | 1.5 | An author-side check, comment hygiene or a checklist issue blocks verification |
142: | 3 | 2 | A command, runtime check or test fails, or a test proves nothing |
143: | 3 | done | Verification evidence is recorded |
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ## 6. RELATED RESOURCES
148: 
149: - [ROUTER.md](../../ROUTER.md) maps intent to resources and declares this file part of the always-loaded preamble.
150: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) covers surface detection and SKILLED language sub-detection.
151: - [`../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md) runs the Phase 1.5 gate.
152: - [`../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md) holds the CI rule evidence and the protected set.
153: - [`../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md) holds the frontend core, the web stack layer and the Figma-to-code check.

14: # Workflow Reference - Verification
15: 
16: Shared `sk-code` doctrine for the final non-mutating evidence phase that gates every done, works, complete, fixed, passing or ready claim.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Verification owns evidence, not fixes. It runs fresh surface-appropriate commands, records the outcomes, compares them against the implementation baseline, names the blind spots and claims only what the evidence proves. When verification fails, it hands back to debugging, implementation or quality without editing.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Verifying work after implementation, quality checks or debugging.
29: - Running final commands before a done, works, complete, fixed, passing or ready claim.
30: - Collecting evidence for active-surface behavior or system-code changes.
31: - Reporting the delta from the baseline captured before implementation.
32: - Running a mutation check or claim falsifier after a green result.
33: - Walking the verification ladder and naming each rung's blind spot.
34: 
35: ### When Not to Use
36: 
37: - The task needs code written, files scaffolded or behavior changed. Use [implementation](./workflow-implement.md).
38: - The task is author-side quality cleanup. Use the `sk-code-quality` mode.
39: - Verification finds a defect that needs root-cause repair. Use [debugging](./workflow-debug.md).
40: - The user wants findings-first review output or PR-style critique. Use the `sk-code-review` mode.
41: - The active surface and verification command set are unknown. Ask for them before claiming anything.
42: 
43: ### Iron Law
44: 
45: **Iron Law**: no completion claim without fresh surface-appropriate verification evidence.
46: 
47: A clean static read is not runtime evidence. A green unit test is not live proof. A successful build is not exercised behavior. One exercised path is not full regression coverage. Name the rung you reached and its blind spot.
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 2. WORKFLOW
52: 
53: ### Verification Loop
54: 
55: 1. Resolve the active surface through [stack-detection.md](../../shared/references/stack-detection.md). If it is unsupported or ambiguous, ask for the verification command set before claiming anything. The quality config, `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet, names quality checks only, so it never supplies the verification command set.
56: 2. Read the implementation, quality or debug handoff for the intended behavior, changed scope, baseline and accepted risks.
57:    - From the quality envelope, read the `checker_outputs` field with the `gate` and `unverified` values it carries, and any field that still reads `PENDING_AGENT_JUDGMENT`.
58:    - Hand back to quality only on `BLOCKED`, `ERROR` or a field still reading `PENDING_AGENT_JUDGMENT`, which is the 3 to 1.5 transition in [phase-detection.md](../../shared/references/phase-detection.md).
59:    - On `UNVERIFIED`, prove each id it lists with this phase's own command or report that id open.
60:    - On `NOTHING_CHECKED`, prove the claim with this phase's own commands and never read the gate as clean, because no check read any file as code, which is where a Markdown-only change lands.
61:    - The run verdict has three readers: this step, the @code RETURN `Quality Gate` field and `sk-code-review`, which reads it as input evidence only.
62: 3. Name the claim to prove and the command, action or observation that proves it.
63: 4. Select the surface-appropriate command set and targeted tests from the active-surface guidance.
64: 5. Run fresh commands and capture the command names, exit codes, test counts, important output and failures.
65: 6. Add end-to-end, runtime or performance evidence when the claim depends on behavior outside static checks.
66: 7. Compare the current evidence to the baseline and report the delta.
67: 8. Run a mutation check or claim falsifier when the claim depends on a new or changed test.
68: 9. Walk the Pre-Claim Gate below, then state only the claims the evidence proves. If the evidence fails, hand back without editing.
69: 
70: ### Baseline And Delta
71: 
72: Verification compares against the baseline whenever it states a no-regressions or improvement claim.
73: 
74: | Field | Required Content |
75: | --- | --- |
76: | Baseline | Starting command status, failing tests, warning count, runtime issue, performance number or `UNKNOWN` when no baseline was captured. |
77: | Current | Fresh output from the whole gate, not only the subset you iterated on: exit codes, test counts, runtime observations or measured numbers. |
78: | Delta | What changed, improved, regressed or remains unproven, including the parts that did not move. |
79: | Claim Scope | The exact claim the evidence supports and the blind spot that remains. |
80: 
81: No baseline means no broad no-regressions claim. A narrower claim tied to fresh evidence still stands.
82: 
83: The baseline floor belongs to `.skilled/repo-rules/evidence-and-proof.md` section 5 (BASELINES). This table is the sk-code record shape for it. Implementation records its Baseline row before the first edit.
84: 
85: ### Verification Ladder
86: 
87: Climb from the cheapest rung to the most authoritative and name what each rung cannot see:
88: 
89: | Rung | Proves | Blind Spot |
90: | --- | --- | --- |
91: | Unit | Isolated logic or assertion path | Integration, wiring, real I/O, runtime state |
92: | In-memory | Multiple modules without external runtime | Real file system, serialization, deployed config, external state |
93: | On-server | Runtime service or local server path | Deployment differences, caches, real user environment |
94: | Live | Exact exercised path in real target | Unexercised paths, other users, other environments, future data |
95: 
96: ### Mutation Check And Claim Falsifier
97: 
98: After green evidence for a new or modified test, confirm the test can fail for the right reason when that is feasible. A true red result is an assertion failing against the intended behavior. A compile error, or a command that never reached the assertion, is not a satisfying red. If a test stays green after the guarded behavior is broken, report it as a verification defect and hand back.
99: 
100: This applies the idea behind `.skilled/repo-rules/evidence-and-proof.md` section 4 (THE NEGATIVE CONTROL): a check that passes whether or not the behavior works proves nothing. The before-fix half of that control, reproducing the failure with the same check, is step 2 of the [Debug Loop](./workflow-debug.md#debug-loop).
101: 
102: ### Pre-Claim Gate Substance
103: 
104: Walk every gate in order before any status claim:
105: 
106: | Gate | Required Discipline |
107: | --- | --- |
108: | Identify | Name the command, action or observation that proves the claim. |
109: | Run | Execute the surface-appropriate verification commands in the current session. |
110: | Test | Exercise targeted unit, integration, end-to-end, runtime or manual checks where available, including at least one edge case and one error path. |
111: | Verify | Confirm the output, exit code, test count and observed behavior match expectations, and that the run reached the changed code on a fresh build with real assertions. |
112: | Record | Save the exact evidence the final claim rests on. |
113: | Claim | State only the narrow claim the evidence supports. |
114: 
115: The Verify row guards against the four ways a green run lies, which `.skilled/repo-rules/evidence-and-proof.md` section 3 lists: it did not run, it ran on the wrong thing, it ran on stale artifacts or it asserted nothing.
116: 
117: ### OpenCode Verification Reality
118: 
119: For system code under `.skilled/` (the `sk-code-skilled` surface), also apply the [verification reality](../../sk-code-skilled/references/shared/workflow-guardrails.md#3-verification-reality), including the `validate.sh` pointer, and the [runtime build traps](../../sk-code-skilled/references/shared/workflow-guardrails.md#4-runtime-build-traps).
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 3. DISCIPLINE
124: 
125: ### Always
126: 
127: - Always run fresh verification in the current session before a completion-related claim.
128: - Always resolve surface identity before selecting commands.
129: - Always record command names, exit codes, key output, test counts and runtime observations.
130: - Always report the baseline, current result, delta and claim scope for a no-regressions or improvement claim.
131: - Always name the verification ladder rung reached and the blind spot that remains.
132: - Always include behavior evidence when runtime behavior changed and tooling is available.
133: - Always hand back when verification finds a defect.
134: - Always confirm the diff scope matches the stated change, with no accidental extras or debug residue.
135: - Always compare warnings against the last working state, so a new warning is reported and not absorbed.
136: 
137: ### Never
138: 
139: - Never edit or create files during verification.
140: - Never dispatch subagents from verification.
141: - Never claim done, works, complete, fixed, passing or ready from unrun commands.
142: - Never claim no regressions without a baseline and a delta.
143: - Never treat one green rung as proof of a higher rung.
144: - Never hide a failed or skipped verifier behind a positive summary.
145: - Never invent runtime, test or performance evidence.
146: - Never verify against stale build output. Clean and rebuild first when an artifact is suspect.
147: - Never present a check run in one environment as proof for every environment.
148: 
149: ### Escalate If
150: 
151: - The surface or the required verification command set is unknown.
152: - A required verifier path is missing or unsafe to run.
153: - Commands contradict each other on a blocking outcome.
154: - Runtime evidence is required but unavailable and the claim would mislead without it.
155: - The baseline is missing and the requested claim needs a regression comparison.
156: - A mutation check shows the test is vacuous.
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: ## 4. HANDOFF BOUNDARIES
161: 
162: - [Debugging](./workflow-debug.md) receives reproducible verification failures, failed commands, broken runtime checks or vacuous tests.
163: - [Implementation](./workflow-implement.md) receives the handback when required behavior is missing or build work is incomplete.
164: - Quality (`sk-code-quality`) receives the handback when author-side checks, comment hygiene or checklist issues block verification.
165: - Review (`sk-code-review`) owns critique when the user wants findings instead of final evidence.
166: 
167: Verification is ready to report only when it ran last, used only non-mutating actions, recorded fresh active-surface evidence, compared against the baseline when the claim needed it, named its blind spots and handed back any defect without editing.
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 5. RELATED RESOURCES
172: 
173: - [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) - the build phase whose baseline and handoff this phase reads.
174: - [workflow-debug.md](./workflow-debug.md) - the repair phase that receives every failed verification.
175: - [stack-detection.md](../../shared/references/stack-detection.md) - surface detection, which decides the command set.
176: - [workflow-guardrails.md](../../sk-code-skilled/references/shared/workflow-guardrails.md) - the verification command chain for system code under `.skilled/`.

19:

21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Debugging is the controlled-experiment phase. It reproduces or tightly characterizes the symptom, captures exact evidence, traces the symptom back to its source, fixes one cause at a time and sends the result back through quality and verification.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Diagnosing a failing test, build failure, runtime exception, console error, broken interaction, output regression, command failure or inconsistent runtime behavior.
29: - Recovering from a failed implementation, quality or verification pass, or from a concrete regression.
30: - Tracing a symptom backward before changing code.
31: - Applying a minimal fix to already-scoped files once the root cause is identified.
32: - Dispatching a bounded parallel investigation when the search space is broad but the symptom is concrete.
33: 
34: ### When Not to Use
35: 
36: - The work is planned implementation or refactoring with no failing symptom. Use [implementation](./workflow-implement.md).
37: - The work is an author-side quality gate with no concrete failing behavior. Use the `sk-code-quality` mode, which runs `quality-gate.cjs` first.
38: - The work is final non-mutating evidence after a fix. Use [verification](./workflow-verify.md).
39: - The user wants findings-first review output instead of a repair. Use the `sk-code-review` mode.
40: - The task is documentation-only prose with no failing behavior.
41: 
42: ### Core Principle
43: 
44: Fix the producer, not the place the symptom surfaced. A patch at the failure site hides the cause and leaves every other reader of the bad value broken.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. WORKFLOW
49: 
50: ### Debug Loop
51: 
52: 1. Resolve the active surface and lifecycle phase through [stack-detection.md](../../shared/references/stack-detection.md) and [phase-detection.md](../../shared/references/phase-detection.md). If the surface is unknown, ask for the runtime and verification commands before changing code.
53: 2. Reproduce the exact symptom with the check that will later prove the fix. If it will not reproduce, collect the exact command, logs, inputs, state or interaction steps needed to narrow it.
54: 3. Capture evidence verbatim: command, exit code, stack trace, console output, failing assertion, path, environment, input or observed behavior.
55: 4. Trace backward from the symptom to the immediate cause, then to the source cause that produced the bad value or state.
56: 5. State the current hypothesis and the evidence that would confirm or refute it.
57: 6. Change one cause at a time and keep the fix as small as the evidence supports.
58: 7. Rerun the original reproduction step after every fix.
59: 8. When the fix changes code, return through quality before final verification.
60: 9. Hand the fixed state to verification with the reproduction command, the before and after results and the residual risk.
61: 
62: The reproduce, trace-to-source and one-cause-at-a-time floors in this loop belong to `.skilled/repo-rules/root-cause-and-debugging.md` section 1 (THE LOOP). The rule that the reproduction uses the same check that will prove the fix belongs to `.skilled/repo-rules/evidence-and-proof.md` section 4 (THE NEGATIVE CONTROL). This loop is how sk-code applies both, so a change to a floor goes there first.
63: 
64: ### Four-Phase Checklist Substance
65: 
66: Walk the four phases in order once a session outlives two trivial fixes:
67: 
68: | Phase | Required Discipline |
69: | --- | --- |
70: | Root Cause Investigation | Reproduce reliably, capture exact output, identify the failing layer, note the last working state and inspect what changed. |
71: | Pattern Analysis | Search the exact error string, separate symptom from cause, trace backward and compare against similar past issues. |
72: | Hypothesis Testing | State one hypothesis, predict the evidence that confirms or refutes it, test one variable and record the observed result. |
73: | Fix | Fix at the source, add or keep regression coverage where it fits and rerun the original reproduction step. |
74: 
75: When an attempt repeats without producing new evidence, stop patching at the failure site. Restate the problem one level up, at the interface, data flow or module boundary, as `.skilled/repo-rules/root-cause-and-debugging.md` section 3 requires.
76: 
77: ### Command Failure Recovery
78: 
79: When a build, test, install or runtime command fails unexpectedly, or a flow that used to work breaks, walk this order before changing code:
80: 
81: 1. **Document.** Capture the full error output, exit code, working directory, relevant environment variables and the last working state (commit, test run or release).
82: 2. **Isolate.** Name the broken layer from the table below before touching it.
83: 3. **Verify prerequisites.** Confirm the working directory, the branch, valid credentials, free disk space, an intact lockfile and a fresh cache. When the cache or lockfile is suspect, reinstall with the package manager's clean-install command and run the tool's clean step.
84: 4. **Retry verbose.** Rerun the failing command with the most verbose flag the tool supports and read the output in order. The first line that differs from a passing run usually names the cause.
85: 5. **Escalate.** After three failed attempts, stop retrying and follow Escalate If below.
86: 
87: | Suspect Layer | First Check |
88: | --- | --- |
89: | Source code | What changed since the last working state (`git diff <last-good>..HEAD`)? |
90: | Build or test tool | The same command with its verbose or debug flag. |
91: | Runtime | The last runtime or dependency version that worked. |
92: | Environment | Required variables set, credentials valid and not expired. |
93: | External service | Its status page, health check or rate limits. |
94: 
95: ### One-Cause Fix Rule
96: 
97: A single edit may touch several lines, but it must address one named cause. Keep unrelated cleanup, speculative hardening and convenience refactors out of a debug fix, because a bundled change leaves the rerun unable to say which edit fixed the symptom. When two independent causes are confirmed, fix and verify them one after the other.
98: 
99: ### Bounded Investigation
100: 
101: Parallel investigation is for bounded diagnosis, never for unsupervised rewriting. The subtask names the exact symptom, the evidence already captured, the files or directories to inspect, the forbidden edits and the expected return shape. Treat its result as a hypothesis until local reproduction confirms it.
102: 
103: ---
104: 
105: ## 3. DISCIPLINE
106: 
107: ### Always
108: 
109: - Always reproduce or tightly characterize the symptom before editing.
110: - Always capture exact evidence instead of paraphrasing a failure.
111: - Always trace the symptom to its source cause before applying a fix.
112: - Always state a one-sentence, evidence-tied root cause before a second fix attempt on the same symptom.
113: - Always change one cause at a time.
114: - Always rerun the original reproduction step after every fix.
115: - Always send changed code through quality before final verification.
116: - Always treat parallel investigation output as a hypothesis until local evidence confirms it.
117: 
118: ### Never
119: 
120: - Never create new files as part of debugging.
121: - Never scaffold planned behavior. Switch to implementation when the requested behavior does not exist.
122: - Never apply several speculative fixes at once.
123: - Never treat a vanished symptom as proof without rerunning the original reproduction step.
124: - Never work around a spec or requirement conflict silently.
125: - Never keep retrying after three failed fixes for the same symptom.
126: - Never claim done, works, fixed, passing or complete from debugging alone. The [Iron Law](./workflow-verify.md#iron-law) gates every completion claim.
127: - Never leave debug instrumentation, such as temporary print or log statements, in the committed fix.
128: 
129: ### Escalate If
130: 
131: - The symptom will not reproduce and the available evidence cannot localize it.
132: - Surface detection is ambiguous or the active runtime is unsupported.
133: - Three fixes fail for the same symptom.
134: - Implementation evidence contradicts an approved spec or user requirement.
135: - Independent validators or reviewers contradict each other on a blocking result.
136: - Security-sensitive validation, filesystem behavior or production data handling is unclear.
137: - A failure involves credentials, tokens or secrets, or would modify production or deployed state. Escalate at once, without retrying.
138: - A failure cascades across unrelated components or fits no reasonable model of the system.
139: 
140: Escalate in the five-part format of `.skilled/repo-rules/root-cause-and-debugging.md` section 7: the symptom verbatim, each attempt with the evidence it produced, what that rules out, two or three options with their trade-offs and one recommendation with its reason.
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ## 4. HANDOFF BOUNDARIES
145: 
146: - [Implementation](./workflow-implement.md) receives the task when the root cause shows the requested behavior was never built or new files are required.
147: - Quality (`sk-code-quality`) receives the changed code after a debug fix. The mode runs `quality-gate.cjs` first, on the files the fix changed.
148: - [Verification](./workflow-verify.md) receives the original reproduction step, the before and after observations, the commands and the residual risks.
149: - Review (`sk-code-review`) owns non-mutating critique when the user wants a diagnosis without a repair.
150: 
151: The handoff is ready when the original symptom is reproduced or characterized, the root cause is tied to evidence, each fix addressed one cause and the original reproduction step now passes, or the escalation explains why it cannot.
152: 
153: ---
154: 
155: ## 5. RELATED RESOURCES
156: 
157: - [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) - the build phase that takes over when the behavior was never implemented.
158: - [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md) - the evidence phase that proves the fix and gates the claim.
159: - [stack-detection.md](../../shared/references/stack-detection.md) - surface detection, read before changing code.
160: - [phase-detection.md](../../shared/references/phase-detection.md) - how a request maps to this phase and what each phase hands on.

All of them read the files below, so each file lives once here instead of being copied into every packet.

25:

15: # Rule Overrides Contract
16: 
17: How a repository or a surface drops or replaces a sk-code rule, and which rules no one can change.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Each repository keeps its own house style. One wants almost no inline comments, and another wants a comment on every function. The quality mode and the review mode ship default rules, and this contract is how a repository or a surface says "not here" or "this instead" for one of them. Both modes read the same section in the same files, so a rule dropped for quality does not come back as a review finding.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - A repository or surface needs to drop or replace a rule outside the hard floor.
30: - A checklist needs a `## Rule overrides` section, or a mode needs to know how one is read and recorded.
31: 
32: ### Core Principle
33: 
34: A repository may change any rule except the hard floor. The floor holds the rules whose breach causes an incident in any codebase, and the review severity scale that every finding is ranked on.
35: 
36: ### Scope
37: 
38: This file defines the format, the ids, the floor, the precedence and how an applied override is recorded.
39: 
40: - The quality and review modes adopt it in their own contracts.
41: - The review mode applies the rows it reads and records them on its `Rule sources` line.
42: - The quality runner reads the section of every checklist it loads through the same linter, applies and records the rows as section 7 describes, and shows the parsed rows and the conflicts in its explain output.
43: - Its registry of known rule ids is read from the documents that declare them, and `commentHygiene.disableRules` carries the machine-checked half.
44: - A mode that does not state that it reads overrides behaves as before.
45: 
46: ### Key Sources
47: 
48: - [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json): the machine-readable hard floor and the machine-checked classes. The linter reads it, and sections 2 and 4 of this file mirror it.
49: - [`../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs`](../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs): the linter that checks a section.
50: - [`../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs`](../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs): the registry of rule ids the quality runner checks a row's id against.
51: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md) section 5: the `<class>.<name>` rule id grammar this contract reuses.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 2. THE SECTION AND ITS ROWS
56: 
57: An override lives in an optional section of a checklist file. The heading reads `## Rule overrides`. A checklist that numbers its headings in upper case may write `## 7. RULE OVERRIDES`, and the linter reads both. The section runs to the next H1 or H2 heading. A file carries at most one.
58: 
59: The section holds one table with three columns:
60: 
61: ```markdown
62: ## Rule overrides
63: 
64: | Rule | Action | Reason |
65: | --- | --- | --- |
66: | `floor.documentation` | none | Public functions carry no doc comments here |
67: | `review.function-length` | replace: A function stays under 60 lines | The team's own limit |
68: ```
69: 
70: | Column | Required | Meaning |
71: | --- | --- | --- |
72: | Rule | Yes | One rule id from section 3. Backticks are optional |
73: | Action | Yes | `none` drops the rule. `replace: <text>` puts the text in its place, with the same severity |
74: | Reason | No | Why the repository differs. A reviewer reads it when the override is recorded |
75: 
76: A row names a single rule, and a section names each rule once. Write a literal pipe in the replacement text as `\|`. Prose lines and fenced examples inside the section are ignored.
77: 
78: A row for a machine-checked id (`hygiene.*`, `debug.*`, `dist.*`) changes what the agent and review apply. The runner's own check changes only through `commentHygiene.disableRules` in the repository's quality config. A `replace:` row on a machine-checked id is refused, because no row can rewrite what the runner matches.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 3. RULE IDS
83: 
84: A rule id is `<class>.<name>`, the grammar of `runner-contract.md` section 5. The class and the name are lower case, and each takes letters, digits and hyphens.
85: 
86: | Class | Names | Source |
87: | --- | --- | --- |
88: | `hygiene`, `conflict`, `secret`, `syntax`, `debug`, `dist` | The runner's own rule names, such as `hygiene.task` | `runner-contract.md` section 5 |
89: | `floor` | One per rule in the universal standards, such as `floor.input-validation` | `code-quality-standards.md` sections 3 to 5 |
90: | `review` | One per rule in the review default lens, such as `review.function-length` | The sk-code-review mode |
91: 
92: A row names a concrete id. A wildcard such as `hygiene.*` is not a row id. The linter checks the grammar, the action and the floor, not whether the id names a rule that exists. Section 7 says what a mode does with an unknown id.
93: 
94: A review check that enforces a rule of the universal floor carries that rule's `floor.*` id, never a `review.*` id, so an override written for the review lens cannot reach a floor rule.
95: 
96: ---
97: 
98: ## 4. THE HARD FLOOR
99: 
100: These ids are fixed. A section that names one is refused. An id ending in `.*` fixes every rule in that class, so a parse rule added later is fixed from the start.
101: 
102: | Id | Rule |
103: | --- | --- |
104: | `syntax.*` | Parse failure: the file does not parse in its language |
105: | `conflict.*` | Merge-conflict markers left in a text file |
106: | `secret.*` | Credential signature: a private-key header or a token in a known format |
107: | `floor.hardcoded-secrets` | No hardcoded secrets: credentials come from the environment or a secret store |
108: | `floor.input-validation` | Input validation: every external input is validated at the boundary |
109: | `floor.silent-failures` | No silent failures: an error reaches the caller or is logged with context |
110: | `floor.initialization-safety` | Initialization safety: setup guards against double init, races and partial loads |
111: | `floor.resource-cleanup` | Resource cleanup: handles, connections, subscriptions and timers close deterministically |
112: | `floor.accessibility` | Accessibility for UI code: keyboard-operable, an accessible name and a visible focus state |
113: | `review.severity` | The review severity ids P0, P1 and P2 and what each one means |
114: | `review.reach` | The review reach rule: a P0 or P1 finding names an input or caller in reach |
115: | `review.security-minimums` | Review security minimums: auth and authorization gaps, injection exposure, unsafe secrets handling and privilege misuse |
116: | `review.correctness-minimums` | Review correctness minimums: regression risk, contract safety, spec mismatch, destructive side effects and boundary handling |
117: 
118: The four `review.*` ids fix the floor of [`review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): its severity ids and reach rule in section 2, and the baseline security and correctness minimums in sections 5 and 6, which that file says surface guidance cannot relax.
119: 
120: Every other rule can be overridden. That covers comment hygiene, documentation, typing strictness, naming, commented-out code, the `ceiling:` marker and every P2 rule. The list above and [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json) hold the same ids, and a test fails when they differ.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 5. PRECEDENCE
125: 
126: When more than one source speaks to the same rule for a file, the higher level wins:
127: 
128: 1. **The hard floor.** No source changes it.
129: 2. **The repository checklist.** A file named in `checklists[]` of the repository's quality config, `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet.
130: 3. **A specific surface.** A hub surface other than SKILLED, or an outside skill that declares a surface.
131: 4. **The SKILLED fallback.** The `sk-code-skilled` checklists.

33:

# Rule: Root cause and debugging

> Routed from [`REPO RULES.md`](../../REPO%20RULES.md). Load when something is red.
> Expands `AGENTS.md`, never overrides it. Where they appear to disagree, `AGENTS.md` wins and this file is wrong. Say so.

## Fires when

- Anything fails: a test, a build, a check, a runtime error, a wrong output.
- You are on the second attempt at the same fix.
- About to add a special case, a retry, a sleep, a broadened `catch`, or a loosened assertion.
- You are tempted to call a failure a flake, an infra problem, or pre-existing.

## The rule

**Fix the producer, not the symptom. Every fix names the mechanism that caused the
failure.**

If you cannot say *why* it broke in one sentence, you have not found the cause, you
have found a place where the symptom stops appearing.

---

## 1. THE LOOP

1. **Reproduce the exact symptom** safely. Not a similar one, the same failure, the
   same message.
2. **Read the whole error.** The top line names where it surfaced; the cause is usually
   the innermost frame in code you control, and the message is usually literal.
3. **Locate the producer:** the code that created the bad value or state, not the code
   that choked on it.
4. **Trace to the consumers.** Anything else reading that producer has the same bug,
   surfaced or not.
5. **Fix at the source.**

- You are tempted to call a failure a flake, an infra problem, or pre-existing.

## The rule

**Fix the producer, not the symptom. Every fix names the mechanism that caused the
failure.**

If you cannot say *why* it broke in one sentence, you have not found the cause, you
have found a place where the symptom stops appearing.

---

## 1. THE LOOP

1. **Reproduce the exact symptom** safely. Not a similar one, the same failure, the
   same message.
2. **Read the whole error.** The top line names where it surfaced; the cause is usually
   the innermost frame in code you control, and the message is usually literal.
3. **Locate the producer:** the code that created the bad value or state, not the code
   that choked on it.
4. **Trace to the consumers.** Anything else reading that producer has the same bug,
   surfaced or not.
5. **Fix at the source.**

5. **Fix at the source.**
6. **Re-run the same check that failed**, then the whole gate.

Step 1 is not optional. If you cannot reproduce it you cannot prove you fixed it, and
you should say so instead of claiming a fix (see the negative control in
`evidence-and-proof.md`).

---

## 2. SYMPTOM-FIX SMELLS

Each is evidence you are patching in the wrong place:

| Smell | What it is really telling you |
|-------|-------------------------------|
| A special case for one caller | The seam between the module and that caller is wrong |
| A retry around a deterministic operation | You do not know why it fails, and now it fails five times |
| A `sleep` | A real ordering or lifecycle bug, now timing-dependent |
| A broadened `catch` or bare `except` | The failure is now silent and the wrong answer ships |
| A widened type or an added `any` | The type was right; the value is wrong |
| Changing the expected value to match the actual | You just wrote the bug down as the specification |
| A default that papers over a missing value | The producer never set it, and now nobody will find out |

---

## 3. WHEN AN ATTEMPT REPEATS

**If an attempt repeats without producing new evidence, stop patching at the failure
site.** The local retry count is set outside this file. This stop fires on repetition
without new evidence, not on a count.

Do not repeat the same guess with a variation. Instead:

1. **Restate the problem one level up:** at the interface, the data flow, or the module
   boundary rather than the line.
2. **Inspect the interface that actually exists.** Read the signature, type, schema,
   docs, caller.
3. **Try once from the new framing.**

Verify commands, flags, paths and APIs exist before relying on them. When an option turns
out unsupported, read the available interface and change approach, do not re-run the
same command with a different spelling.

**Naming the seam.** When a fix only works by special-casing a caller, the boundary is
wrong. Say so: **name the seam and the files a seam fix would touch**, then ask.
`scope-discipline.md` still binds, "the real fix is over there" does not grant a yes.

---

## 4. NEVER MAKE A CHECK PASS BY WEAKENING IT

Not a fix, in any circumstance: skipping, disabling, quarantining or deleting a failing
test; loosening an assertion until it passes; excluding the failing file from the linter,
type checker or matcher; committing an empty change or re-triggering a run for a
different roll.

If a test is genuinely wrong, that is a finding to raise with evidence, not a line to
edit on your way past.

---

## 5. "FLAKE" IS A CONCLUSION, NOT A STARTING HYPOTHESIS

Only two things support it: the same check passed on this exact input before, or the run
died before any test body executed (checkout, install, runner loss). Absent one of those,
treat the failure as real. One re-run to confirm, at most; a second failure is a bug.

---

## 6. OWNERSHIP

# Skill ARCHITECTURE.md Template

Use this template for the `ARCHITECTURE.md` at a skill package root, next to `SKILL.md` and `README.md`. It explains how the package's code works as a system. The README orients a user, `SKILL.md` routes an agent, and `ARCHITECTURE.md` tells a maintainer where behavior lives and which way dependencies run.

---

## 1. WHEN TO USE

Write an `ARCHITECTURE.md` when a skill package ships runtime code: a daemon, a CLI, a library, hooks or scripts with more than one layer. A documentation-only skill does not need one.

A code-folder README (`readme-code-template.md`) covers one folder. `ARCHITECTURE.md` covers the whole package: how its zones relate, the paths data takes through them, and what enforces the contract. When a folder README starts explaining other folders, that explanation belongs here.

---

## 2. CONTENT MODEL

The eight sections are fixed and numbered in this order, so a reader moving between skills finds the same thing in the same place. A section with nothing to say states that in one line rather than disappearing.

| Section | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1. OVERVIEW | What the package does, its front door, its authored zones, and an architecture diagram | One or two paragraphs plus the diagram |
| 2. PACKAGE TOPOLOGY | A directory tree of the package with one-line roles, and the allowed dependency direction | Show only folders that matter; list import edges as `a/ ──▶ b/` |
| 3. CANONICAL FLOWS | The main read path and write path, each named after its entry command, plus the module that owns each | Keep to the paths that define the package |
| 4. RUNTIME SUBSYSTEMS | One bolded paragraph per subsystem: what it does and where it lives | Link reference docs for depth instead of repeating them |
| 5. HOOK AND PLUGIN INTEGRATION | How runtimes, hooks, plugins or other skills call in, and what happens on timeout or failure | Write "None" when the package has no integration surface |
| 6. ENFORCEMENT AND VERIFICATION | The checks that hold the contract: validators, test suites, benchmarks, playbooks | Name the command or folder for each |
| 7. DECISION RECORDS | A table of the architecture decisions still in force, with status | Local numbering only; no spec or packet ids |
| 8. RELATED | Links to README, SKILL.md, install guide, feature catalog, playbook and references | Relative links from the package root |

---
